This is a full-length practice exam **with solutions**. It mirrors the real midterm
(Thursday, October 15, in the lecture slot) in length, difficulty, coverage, and
format; the real exam asks *different* questions from the same topics. Print this
page (solutions expand automatically in print), sit it in one honest 90-minute
block with pen and paper, and only then read the solutions — see the
[review page](midterm.qmd) for how to study from your mistakes.

**Rules on the day** (same as printed on the real cover page): closed book, no
notes, no devices, no calculator — every computation is designed for pen and
paper. Multiple-choice questions have exactly one best answer. Open questions are
graded for the reasoning, not just the final number. Each question is worth 2
points; 20 questions, 40 points total.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Representations (Weeks 1–2)

**Q1 (open).** The weighted adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is

$$
W = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1.5 & 0 & 2.0\\
1.5 & 0 & 0.5 & 0\\
0 & 0.5 & 0 & 3.0\\
2.0 & 0 & 3.0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Draw the graph, and compute its **average degree** (degree = number of incident
edges, ignoring weights).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Nonzero entries above the diagonal give the edge list: $(1,2)$ w 1.5, $(1,4)$ w
2.0, $(2,3)$ w 0.5, $(3,4)$ w 3.0 — a 4-cycle $1\!-\!2\!-\!3\!-\!4\!-\!1$ with 4
edges. Average degree $= 2E/N = 8/4 = \mathbf{2}$ (every node has degree exactly 2
here). Common slip: counting each symmetric entry as its own edge and getting 4.
:::

**Q2 (MCQ).** Two adjacency matrices $A_1$ and $A_2$ of the same size have
identical degree sequences but different entries. Which statement is correct?

a. They necessarily describe the same graph, written in different node orders.
b. They necessarily describe different graphs.
c. They *may* describe the same graph under a node relabeling — matching degree
   sequences are necessary but not sufficient evidence.
d. They describe the same graph if and only if $A_1$ and $A_2$ have the same trace.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(c).** A permutation $P$ relabels a graph as $PAP^\top$ without changing the
degree multiset, so *same graph* is possible — but two genuinely different graphs
can also share a degree sequence (a 6-cycle and two triangles both have all
degrees 2), so it is not guaranteed. (a) and (b) each claim certainty the evidence
cannot give; (d) is irrelevant — simple graphs all have trace 0.
:::

## Classical graph ML (Week 2)

**Q3 (open).** For the graph below, compute: the **degree of every node**, the
**clustering coefficient of C**, the **closeness centrality of C** (normalized,
$\frac{n-1}{\sum_u d(C,u)}$), and the **betweenness of C** (unnormalized: the
number of shortest paths between other pairs that pass through C, counting each
pair once).

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-mt-centrality.html >}}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Degrees: A 2, B 2, **C 3**, D 2, E 1. Clustering of C: neighbors $\{A,B,D\}$ form
$\binom{3}{2}=3$ possible pairs, of which one (A–B) is an edge → $\mathbf{1/3}$.
Closeness of C: distances 1, 1, 1, 2 to A, B, D, E → $4/5 = \mathbf{0.8}$.
Betweenness of C: the pairs (A,D), (A,E), (B,D), (B,E) each have a *unique*
shortest path, and each runs through C → $\mathbf{4}$. (Pairs inside the triangle
use their direct edge; (D,E) is an edge.)
:::

**Q4 (open).** For the directed graph below, run **two power iterations** of
simplified PageRank (no teleport): start from $r^{(0)} = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13,
\tfrac13)$ and split each node's rank equally over its out-links. Then find the
**fixed point** — the ranks that no longer change.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-mt-pagerank.html >}}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Out-degrees: X 1, Y 2, Z 1. Each round: X collects half of Y plus all of Z; Y
collects all of X; Z collects half of Y.

$$r^{(1)} = \left(\tfrac16+\tfrac13,\; \tfrac13,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac16\right), \qquad
r^{(2)} = \left(\tfrac16+\tfrac16,\; \tfrac12,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac13, \tfrac12, \tfrac16\right).$$

Fixed point: solve $r_X = \tfrac12 r_Y + r_Z$, $r_Y = r_X$, $r_Z = \tfrac12 r_Y$
with $r_X+r_Y+r_Z=1$: $\mathbf{(2/5,\ 2/5,\ 1/5)}$ — check: $\tfrac15+\tfrac15 =
\tfrac25$. ✓
:::

**Q5 (MCQ).** Real PageRank adds a teleport term,

$$r = \beta M r + (1-\beta)\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}.$$

What goes wrong *without* it?

a. Power iteration diverges to infinity on any graph with a cycle.
b. Spider traps (groups with no way out) absorb all rank, and dead ends (no
   out-links) leak rank out of the system entirely.
c. The computation becomes quadratic in the number of edges.
d. Rank becomes proportional to in-degree, which is trivial.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** Both pathologies are absorption/leakage problems of the pure random walk;
teleport makes the chain irreducible and aperiodic, guaranteeing one positive
stationary distribution. (a) is impossible — the update conserves total rank
(dead ends *shrink* it, never grow it); (c) confuses convergence with cost per
iteration; (d) is false in general — PageRank on the Q4 graph is not ordered by
in-degree alone.
:::

**Q6 (open).** Run **Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement** on the two graphs below,
both starting from uniform colors. Give the color histograms after rounds 1
and 2, state when refinement stabilizes, and say what the WL test concludes —
and whether that conclusion is *correct*.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-mt-wl.html >}}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every node in both graphs has degree 2, so after round 1 every node has collected
the same multiset $\{c_0, c_0\}$ and receives the same new color: histogram
$\{6\}$ in both graphs. Round 2 repeats the situation — the partition never
splits, so refinement is stable after one round. WL therefore reports **"possibly
isomorphic."** That conclusion is *wrong*: $G_1$ is disconnected and $G_2$ is a
single cycle. This is the standard demonstration that WL is **sound but not
complete** — identical histograms prove nothing, only *different* histograms
prove non-isomorphism.
:::

## Shallow embeddings (Week 3)

**Q7 (MCQ).** In node2vec, walks are biased by the return parameter $p$ and
in-out parameter $q$. Setting $q \ll 1$ (with $p$ moderate) produces walks that…

a. …stay close to the start node, capturing local structural roles.
b. …wander outward, DFS-style, so embeddings capture community membership.
c. …revisit the previous node often, approximating breadth-first search.
d. …become uniform random walks, recovering DeepWalk exactly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** Small $q$ makes *moving away* from the previous node cheap, so walks
range across the community — nodes far apart in the same region co-occur, and the
embedding encodes homophily. (a)/(c) describe the opposite regime (small $p$,
BFS-like); (d) requires $p = q = 1$, not $q \ll 1$.
:::

**Q8 (open).** The skip-gram objective replaces the full softmax with negative
sampling:

$$\log \sigma(z_u^\top z_v) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{n_i \sim P_n}\!\left[\log \sigma(-z_u^\top z_{n_i})\right].$$

Explain the role of each of the two terms, why this approximates the softmax at a
tiny fraction of its cost, and what role $k$ plays.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first term pushes the embeddings of nodes that *do* co-occur on walks toward
high inner product; the second pushes $u$ away from $k$ *sampled* non-neighbors.
The full softmax normalizes over all $n$ nodes — $O(n)$ per update — precisely so
that raising one similarity implicitly lowers the rest; negative sampling makes
that competition explicit with $k$ sampled contrast points, at cost $O(k)$,
$k \approx 5\text{–}20$. Larger $k$ gives a lower-variance gradient (and shifts
the fixed point: SGNS factorizes PMI shifted by $\log k$); $k$ trades compute for
statistical sharpness — it is not a regularizer, and $k=0$ collapses the loss
(everything can be pushed to similarity 1).
:::

**Q9 (MCQ).** You learn DeepWalk embeddings on a co-authorship graph, then
evaluate link prediction on a random 10% of edges you hid *after* learning. Your
AUC is suspiciously excellent. The most likely explanation is:

a. DeepWalk is simply an excellent link predictor on co-authorship data.
b. The walks were generated on the full graph, so the "hidden" edges shaped the
   embeddings — the evaluation leaks.
c. AUC is the wrong metric for link prediction under class imbalance.
d. The embedding dimension was too large, causing overfitting.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** Test edges must be removed *before* walk generation; walks that crossed
a test edge deposit exactly the co-occurrence signal the evaluation then
"predicts." In Lab 3 this leak inflated AUC from 0.824 to 0.997 on Cora — an
effect far larger than any modeling choice. (a) explains nothing suspicious; (c)
is a real concern but affects both honest and leaky pipelines equally; (d) would
depress, not inflate, test performance.
:::

## Knowledge graphs (Week 4)

**Q10 (open).** A TransE model has 2-dimensional embeddings: $e_{\text{Inno}} =
(1,0)$, $e_{\text{Tat}} = (1,1)$, $e_{\text{Mos}} = (3,2)$, and
$r_{\text{located\_in}} = (0,1)$. Using the score $-\lVert h + r - t\rVert$,
which of the triples (Inno, located_in, Tat) and (Inno, located_in, Mos) does the
model prefer, and by what distances? Then prove in one line: TransE with
$r \neq 0$ cannot make a relation **symmetric** (both $(a,r,b)$ and $(b,r,a)$
scoring perfectly).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$h + r = (1,1)$. Distance to Tat: $\lVert (1,1)-(1,1)\rVert = \mathbf{0}$
(perfect). Distance to Mos: $\lVert (1,1)-(3,2)\rVert = \sqrt{4+1} =
\mathbf{\sqrt5} \approx 2.24$. The model prefers (Inno, located_in, Tat).
Symmetry proof: perfect scores mean $a + r = b$ and $b + r = a$; adding the two
equations gives $2r = 0$, contradicting $r \neq 0$. $\square$
:::

**Q11 (MCQ).** DistMult scores a triple as $\langle h, r, t\rangle = \sum_i h_i
r_i t_i$. Its structural limitation is that it…

a. …cannot model any relation that is transitive.
b. …assigns every relation the same score to $(h,r,t)$ and $(t,r,h)$, so it
   cannot represent one-directional facts.
c. …requires all embeddings to be non-negative.
d. …cannot be trained with negative sampling.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** The trilinear product is unchanged by swapping $h$ and $t$, so every
relation is forced symmetric — *supervises*, *capital_of*, *parent_of* are all
beyond it, which is why ComplEx moves to complex conjugation. In HW1 you caught
this on camera: after 1,500 training steps the forward/reverse score gap was
$\sim 2\times10^{-7}$. (a) is false (symmetry, not transitivity, is the issue);
(c) and (d) are simply untrue.
:::

**Q12 (open).** For the query $(h, r, ?)$ your model scores five candidate tails:
$t_1: 0.9$, $t_2: 0.8$, $t_3: 0.7$, $t_4: 0.6$, $t_5: 0.5$ (higher is better).
The correct answer is $t_3$. The training set also contains the true triple
$(h, r, t_1)$. Compute the **raw rank** and the **filtered rank** of $t_3$, and
say in one sentence why filtered is the honest one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Raw: two candidates outscore $t_3$ → rank $\mathbf{3}$. Filtered: $t_1$ is a
*known true answer*, so it is removed from the competition; only $t_2$ remains
above → rank $\mathbf{2}$. Filtering is honest because the model should not be
punished for ranking a *different correct answer* above the test answer — raw
rank penalizes knowledge, filtered rank penalizes only genuine mistakes.
:::

## Multi-hop reasoning (Week 5)

**Q13 (MCQ).** Query2box embeds queries as boxes rather than points chiefly
because…

a. …boxes have more parameters, so they fit the training data better.
b. …a conjunction of queries becomes an intersection of regions, and boxes are
   closed under intersection while points cannot represent an answer *set* at all.
c. …box distance is faster to compute than point distance.
d. …boxes eliminate the need for negative sampling.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** A query's answer is a *set* of entities; a region can contain a set, a
point cannot. Conjunction ("drugs that target COX **and** treat inflammation")
requires intersecting answer sets, and the intersection of axis-aligned boxes is
again an axis-aligned box — representation closed under the operator the problem
demands. That closure argument, not capacity (a) or speed (c), is the design
principle of the whole Week 5 arc.
:::

**Q14 (open).** A user asks: *"Which mentor of our lab's founder also worked at
Bell Labs?"* Explain why plain vector-similarity retrieval (embed the question,
fetch nearest documents) tends to fail here, and what a GraphRAG-style system
does instead. Two or three sentences.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The answer lives at the end of a *chain* — founder → mentor → employer — and no
single document need be similar to the question text; similarity retrieval
fetches documents about "our lab" or "Bell Labs" but the connecting entity may
appear in neither. A GraphRAG system resolves the question to a starting entity,
*traverses* typed edges (founded_by, mentored_by, worked_at) to assemble the
chain, and hands the resulting subgraph to the language model as context — the
graph supplies the multi-hop structure that embedding similarity cannot.
:::

## GCN (Week 6)

**Q15 (open).** For the path graph $1 - 2 - 3$, form $\hat A =
\tilde D^{-1/2}(A+I)\tilde D^{-1/2}$ and propagate the feature vector $x =
(1, 0, 0)^\top$ one step (identity weights, no nonlinearity). Give all three
output values exactly and interpret the zero.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Degrees with self-loops: $\tilde d = (2, 3, 2)$. The nonzero entries of $\hat A$:
$\hat A_{11} = \tfrac12$, $\hat A_{12} = \hat A_{21} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}$,
$\hat A_{22} = \tfrac13$, $\hat A_{23} = \hat A_{32} = \tfrac1{\sqrt6}$,
$\hat A_{33} = \tfrac12$. So

$$\hat A x = \left(\tfrac12,\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\; 0\right) \approx (0.5,\; 0.408,\; 0).$$

Node 3 stays at **0** because it is two hops from the signal and one layer moves
information exactly one hop — the receptive-field fact that motivates stacking
layers (and, at depth, invites oversmoothing).
:::

**Q16 (MCQ).** Stacking many plain GCN propagation layers (no residuals) makes
node representations collapse toward each other. The mechanism is:

a. Vanishing gradients prevent the deep layers from training.
b. Repeated multiplication by $\hat A$ is a low-pass filter — components along
   all non-dominant eigenvectors decay geometrically, leaving features
   proportional to a single dominant direction.
c. The ReLU nonlinearity saturates after ~4 layers.
d. Self-loops accumulate, making every node its own dominant neighbor.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** $\hat A$'s spectrum lies in $(-1, 1]$ with the top eigenvector
$\propto \tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf 1$; powers of $\hat A$ kill every other component
at rate $|\lambda_i|^K$. This happens *even with no training at all* — it is a
property of the propagation operator, which is why the Week 7 repair shop fixes
it architecturally (residuals, restart) rather than with a better optimizer (a).
:::

**Q17 (MCQ).** Give both graphs of Q6 uniform node features (every node the
vector $\mathbf 1$). A GCN of *any* depth produces node embeddings on $G_1$ (two
triangles) and $G_2$ (hexagon) such that:

a. Sufficient depth eventually separates the two graphs.
b. Every node in both graphs gets the *same* embedding, so any pooled graph
   representation is identical — the GCN provably cannot tell them apart.
c. The graphs are separated if and only if mean pooling is replaced by max.
d. The GCN separates them because their Laplacian spectra differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** With identical features and identical degrees everywhere, every node
sees the same self-value and the same neighbor multiset at every layer — the
computation graphs are indistinguishable, so all node embeddings stay equal
(this is exactly the WL argument of Q6 in linear-algebra clothes: message
passing is bounded by WL). Depth doesn't help (a), pooling can't separate equal
multisets of equal vectors (c), and the GCN never sees the spectrum (d) —
spectral *fingerprints* from HW1 do separate this pair, which is the point of
contrasting them.
:::

## The design space (Week 7)

**Q18 (open).** Two neighborhoods have one-hot features $t = (1,0)$, $g = (0,1)$.
For each pair below, mark which of **mean / max / sum** aggregators are *confused*
(produce identical outputs) and which *separate* the pair:

| pair | mean | max | sum |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\{t\}$ vs $\{t, t\}$ | | | |
| $\{t,t,g\}$ vs $\{t,g,g\}$ | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Row 1: mean $(1,0)$ vs $(1,0)$ **confused**; max $(1,0)$ vs $(1,0)$ **confused**;
sum $(1,0)$ vs $(2,0)$ **separates** — only sum sees multiplicity. Row 2: mean
$(\tfrac23,\tfrac13)$ vs $(\tfrac13,\tfrac23)$ **separates**; max $(1,1)$ vs
$(1,1)$ **confused**; sum $(2,1)$ vs $(1,2)$ **separates**. Moral: over one-hot
(countable) features sum dominates — it recovers the exact multiset — which is
why GIN aggregates with sum; mean keeps proportions, max keeps only support.
:::

**Q19 (open).** GAT scores an edge as

$$e_{vu} = \text{LeakyReLU}\!\left(\mathbf a^\top [\mathbf W h_v \,\Vert\, \mathbf W h_u]\right).$$

State the **static attention** limitation this creates (one sentence identifying
*what* cannot be expressed), and give the GATv2 repair (one line).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Split $\mathbf a^\top[\cdot\Vert\cdot]$ into a receiver term plus a sender term:
for a fixed receiver, the *ranking* of senders is determined by the sender term
$\mathbf a_2^\top \mathbf W h_u$ alone — the **same ranking for every receiver**
— so no pattern where different receivers prefer different senders (e.g., "query
$i$ attends to key $i$") is expressible. GATv2 moves the nonlinearity inside:
$e_{vu} = \mathbf a^\top \text{LeakyReLU}\!\left(\mathbf W [h_v \Vert
h_u]\right)$, letting receiver and sender interact before the score, which kills
the separation argument.
:::

**Q20 (MCQ).** GraphSAGE can embed a node that did not exist during training;
DeepWalk cannot. The reason is:

a. GraphSAGE trains longer, so it generalizes better.
b. DeepWalk's parameters *are* the per-node embedding table, while GraphSAGE
   learns aggregation functions applied to node features — new node, same
   functions.
c. GraphSAGE stores the training graph and looks up the nearest known node.
d. DeepWalk could do it too if the walks were long enough.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** This is the inductive/transductive divide: DeepWalk's only knowledge is
a learned vector per training node — an unseen node has no row in the table and
no walks behind it. GraphSAGE's knowledge is *how to compute* an embedding from a
neighborhood's features, so it applies unchanged to nodes (or entire graphs)
never seen in training. (d) is false in principle, not just in practice: no walk
statistics exist for a node absent from the graph.
:::

## After you sit it

Score yourself: 2 points per question, partial credit on open questions for
correct method with arithmetic slips. **32+/40** — you are ready; review only
what you missed. **24–31** — solid; redo the missed topics' lecture self-checks
and the corresponding lab exercises. **Below 24** — work back through the
[review page](midterm.qmd) checklist week by week, labs before lectures. Every
solution above names the lecture concept it tests, so a wrong answer points at
exactly one thing to re-read.
